ESIDIMENI HEARINGS

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The last three weeks have seen the harrowing unfolding of testimony in the Esidimeni arbitration hearings...are we truly grasping the scale of the tragedy? What will arbitration really mean?

Unique Selling Point:
In scenes strongly reminiscent of the truth and reconciliation commission that sought, after apartheid, to deal with the excesses of the state...South Africa has sat in the last three weeks to listen to live streaming of the public hearing in the Esidimeni tragedy. Over two years of unfolding tragedy the body count has steadily risen. It’s now at 141.
Witness after witness has told of the dire neglect, callous disregard of warnings and brutal treatment that their loved ones have received at the hands of the Gauteng Department of Health -- all as a result of the decision and actions of former MEC Qedani Mahlangu and her top team. We recap three weeks of testimony and the pat answers and formulaic responses of government lawyers.

Press Release:


With over 100 psychiatric patients confirmed dead at the hands of the Gauteng Health Department, former Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu still hasn’t testified at the Life Esidimeni arbitration hearings. As devastated families continue to search for answers, will the hearings finally bring closure?

Script:


VO: In scenes reminiscent of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, arbitration hearings into the Life Esidimeni tragedy have for three weeks heard heartbreaking testimony about psychiatric patients callously neglected and their families disregarded.

CHRISTINE NXUMALO: It’s been a very long road - painful, very long road.

VO: Carte Blanche first met Christine Nxumalo last year - she was desperately trying to track down her sister, Virginia Machpelah.

STRAP: CARTE BLANCHE SEPTEMBER 2016: CHRISTINE NXUMALO: My sister may not mean anything to anybody else, but she’s my sister. She means to me the world. They had no right to do that.

VO: Virginia was one of the one-thousand-seven-hundred people moved to unlicensed and ill-equipped NGOs when the Gauteng Health Department terminated its contract with Life Esidimeni, a private hospital specialising in long-term patient care. Qedani Mahlangu, then Gauteng Health MEC, said it was to cut costs and to implement a new policy to deinstitutionalise psychiatric care.

DEVI LINK: In October 2015 the Gauteng Department of Health announced that the move had been finalised -- this despite the loud protests from various organisations and family members.

VO: Public interest law centre Section27 and its director, Mark Heywood, fought the move.

MARK HEYWOOD, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, SECTION27: We spent a lot of 2015 trying to persuade the Gauteng Government not to close the facility. We went to court to try to stop the closure of Life Esidimeni. We lost in court. And then they started to move people and then people started to die…

VO: Nxumalo eventually learned that her sister had died at Precious Angels NGO in Pretoria. Of 58 patients moved there, 23 died. In his report on the tragedy, health ombudsman Prof. Malegapuru Makgoba found it was not the only NGO where Esidimeni patients died due to neglect.

DEVI LINK: When Mahlangu reported to the legislature in September 2016 the body count was 36 -- which went up to 94 in February this year after the Ombudsman released his report -- but by last week the body count had shot up to a 141.

VO: This week, Nxumalo told her story at the arbitration hearings that the families of those who died, had called for in order to get desperately needed answers.

CHRISTINE NXUMALO: Our understanding that when we started the arbitration process that we were going to get answers. But all the officials, they have not offered any answers and that makes me angry. They were protecting themselves.

VO: Retired deputy chief justice Dikgang Moseneke was chosen to lead the process. Parties agreed to abide by his decisions.

DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: When I speak to you, Mark, there never any boundaries, but this time there are. Explain what they are and why?

MARK HEYWOOD, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, SECTION27: Section 27 is the legal representative of 60 families of people who died. We’re very much at the heart of this process. And so we are compelled to respect the boundaries of the process that had been set by Justice Moseneke. And I think not to prejudge the outcomes. You know, the people who have suffered are speaking for themselves. The Government officials are being made to account, are being made to answer questions about...about what happened and we have to allow this process to unfold, rather than for me to do what I normally do, which is tell you exactly what I think.

VO: Katharine Child, reporter for The Times, has interviewed many of the families.

KATHARINE CHILD, REPORTER, THE TIMES: To hear one family member after the next...It began to feel like a holocaust movie. You just begin to sit there and your stomach will turn and you feel sick and you think, no, it can’t get any worse. You start to whisper under your breath or listen to the audience just getting really angry.

MARK HEYWOOD, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, SECTION27: There’s just so much sorrow in the room itself. And occasionally when the story is recounted, somebody cannot contain themselves anymore, tears to flow and then it’s like a ripple effect.

ADILA HASSIM: Did you identify Joseph’s body?

NTHOMBIFUTHI DLADLA: I didn’t want to go and identify his body, but Daphney insisted that I do so.

VO: Ntombifuthi Dladla’s brother Joseph Gumede was taken to Life Esidimeni after he became violent at home. He would roam the streets. He died in July 2016 at an NGO, but his family was only told seven months later.

JUDGE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: You said that his body was a painful sight to look at...

NTHOMBIFUTHI DLADLA: He said I want you to come and see your brother’s body because now maggots were coming out of the body.

JUDGE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Sometimes the truth becomes necessary even if it is this painful.

NTHOMBIFUTHI DLADLA: What hurt me the most is that I tried to take my brother to a place of safety only to find out I would be the one to sign off his death.

LUCAS MOGOERANE: This is a wakeup call. We want to see appropriate counselling, very fair and good compensation.

VO: Despite suffering from schizophrenia, Lucas Mogoerane’s brother, Christopher, was strong. After being moved from Esidimeni to an NGO, he wasted away in just two weeks.

LUCAS MOGOERANE: We want to see a memorial monument - to be in the history since the inception of this government - this is four times the Marikana...This shouldn’t happen. This follows the words of Madiba saying never and never and never again should this happen.

VO: These crosses by the side of the road in Kyalami, Johannesburg, is so far the only monument to the deceased -- a tribute by nursery owner Bill Rutherford and his employees.

BILL RUTHERFORD: The whole episode is so horrifying for me and it’s just beyond belief. And I put it up just as a memorial to those people. Since then we’ve had enormous response from the public who come in now all the time. Many people cry. It made me feel that there are so many people who care and one of these days we will get the authorities to care as well.

VO: They’re now making black crosses for 59 patients still missing after the move.

DEVI LINK: Many of the family members attending the hearings are expecting answers but at this stage there are many more questions.

VO: The owner of Precious Angels, where Virginia Machpelah and 22 others died, testified. Ethel Ncube denied her facility was inadequate and blamed Gauteng Health for failing to provide money and support.

ETHEL NCUBE, OWNER, PRECIOUS ANGELS NGO: I exhausted savings as well for my little one and opted not to pay rent. I had to be kicked out, just for me to save and get diapers and get food.

VO: Numerous government officials have testified of rushed plans pushed through despite warnings. Many offered apologies to the families.

DEVI LINK: In August last year when we sat down with the then MEC for health Qedani Mahlangu we were concerned about 6 suspected deaths -- 15 months later and we’re looking at close to a 150.

STRAP: INTERVIEW AUGUST 2016: DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: We’ve got a few relapsed cases, but we…
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: I do not remember any information …
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: … since June … nothing?
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: … of any patients being relapsing in this. The patients who died, I think some died at Life, I think it was about 6 patients I heard that died just the move was happening or just before the move happened or just maybe on arrival at those places.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: SASOP, SADAG and Section 27 went to court December?
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: No, no, there was a court ruling when we started placing patients in Takalani and the court dismissed their thing, I can’t remember ...
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: They say these are the exact issues they were trying to raise with the department before this process went ahead.
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: I don’t know you preempt issues in January ...
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: Because they can see it coming.
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: Okay, unless they were foretellers.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: No, they say it was practical enough that they could see this problem coming.
MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: Well, I don’t know. I just believe in our quest to do what’s right we will make mistakes and we will take full responsibility for those mistakes that have been committed through this process and it’s not because we are trying to be malicious or trying to hurt anybody…

VO: Mahlangu resigned in February, just before the health ombud’s report, that questioned her leadership, was released. National director-general for health Precious Matsoso called for Mahlangu to testify.

PRECIOUS MATSOSO, DIRECTOR-GENERAL, HEALTH: I would have thought that a particular individual would have been called to give answers. Some of the answers could not have been given by Mosenogi as a junior official, some of the questions I can’t answer myself because that project was executed wrongfully.

ADILA HASSIM: Are there any other government officials you want to hear from?

CHRISTINE NXUMALO: Obviously we want to hear from Qedani Mahlangu, she needs to come and testify. She needs to come and tell us what happened - she signed off on all of this as the MEC and the HOD as well.

DEVI LINK: But where is Qedani Mahlangu? She’s studying at the London school of Economics and according to the Gauteng Department of Health she is willing to come and testify but only after she’s written her exams.

KATHARINE CHILD, REPORTER, THE TIMES: What we do know is that she started studying in September. It’s a UK course, it’s post-grad. It’s unlikely that she’s got exams a month into her course. So, will she come? Will she tell the truth?

VO: In an interview broadcast on Talk Radio 702 this past week, Mahlangu said events have been hard on her.

UPS QEDANI MAHLANGU, RADIO INTERVIEW, : ...you do so much in trying to do what is right. No one says it’s going to be easy to lead. It’s not been an easy journey.

MARK HEYWOOD: Like Marikana, I think the roots of this are in political negligence of one form or another and I think that the country has to understand the implications of Life Esidimeni.

PROMOS:

10 secs
VO: With the body count stacking up in the Esidimeni tragedy...is the unfolding arbitration process providing the answers and accountability to bring peace to the families?

15 secs
VO: Will former Gauteng Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu return to tell of her part in the Esidimeni tragedy that led to the death of at least 141 people?
CHRISTINE NXUMALO: Obviously we want to hear from Qedani Mahlangu, she needs to come and testify...

15 secs
KATHARINE CHILD, REPORTER, THE TIMES: To hear one family member after the next...It began to feel like a holocaust movie… you just began to sit there and your stomach would turn and you’d feel sick.
VO: Can families devastated by the Esidimeni tragedy find closure in the arbitration process?

QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG HEALTH MEC: Okay, unless they were foretellers. DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: No, they say it was practical enough that they could see this problem coming. MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: Well, I don’t know. I just believe in our quest to do what’s right we will make mistakes and we will take full responsibility for those mistakes that have been committed through this process and it’s not because we are trying to be malicious or trying to hurt anybody… VO: Mahlangu resigned in February, just before the health ombud’s report, that questioned her leadership, was released. National director-general for health Precious Matsoso called for Mahlangu to testify. PRECIOUS MATSOSO, DIRECTOR-GENERAL, HEALTH: I would have thought that a particular individual would have been called to give answers. Some of the answers could not have been given by Mosenogi as a junior official, some of the questions I can’t answer myself because that project was executed wrongfully. ADILA HASSIM: Are there any other government officials you want to hear from? CHRISTINE NXUMALO: Obviously we want to hear from Qedani Mahlangu, she needs to come and testify. She needs to come and tell us what happened - she signed off on all of this as the MEC and the HOD as well. DEVI LINK: But where is Qedani Mahlangu? She’s studying at the London school of Economics and according to the Gauteng Department of Health she is willing to come and testify but only after she’s written her exams. KATHARINE CHILD, REPORTER, THE TIMES: What we do know is that she started studying in September. It’s a UK course, it’s post-grad. It’s unlikely that she’s got exams a month into her course. So, will she come? Will she tell the truth? VO: In an interview broadcast on Talk Radio 702 this past week, Mahlangu said events have been hard on her. UPS QEDANI MAHLANGU, RADIO INTERVIEW, : ...you do so much in trying to do what is right. No one says it’s going to be easy to lead. It’s not been an easy journey. MARK HEYWOOD: Like Marikana, I think the roots of this are in political negligence of one form or another and I think that the country has to understand the implications of Life Esidimeni. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The last three weeks have seen the harrowing unfolding of testimony in the Esidimeni arbitration hearings...are we truly grasping the scale of the tragedy? What will arbitration really mean?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In scenes strongly reminiscent of the truth and reconciliation commission that sought, after apartheid, to deal with the excesses of the state...South Africa has sat in the last three weeks to listen to live streaming of the public hearing in the Esidimeni tragedy. Over two years of unfolding tragedy the body count has steadily risen. It’s now at 141. Witness after witness has told of the dire neglect, callous disregard of warnings and brutal treatment that their loved ones have received at the hands of the Gauteng Department of Health -- all as a result of the decision and actions of former MEC Qedani Mahlangu and her top team. We recap three weeks of testimony and the pat answers and formulaic responses of government lawyers.
